# Deuteronomy Chapter 6 — SOPHIA Consensus Translation
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **Sources:** EMET (Literal), LOGOS (Formal), PNEUMA (Dynamic)
**Hebrew Base:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 203–204
**LXX Reference:** Codex Vaticanus (Vat.gr.1209), pp. 148
**Disagreement Log:** `disagreements/DEU_006.md`

---

## Council Notes

Chapter 6 is the theological pinnacle of Deuteronomy's first address and arguably of the entire Pentateuch. It opens with the purpose of the commandment (vv.1–3), delivers the Shema (v.4) and the great love command (v.5), grounds these in household and bodily practice (vv.6–9), warns against the spiritual danger of prosperity (vv.10–12), prohibits allegiance to other gods on pain of destruction (vv.13–15), reinforces the prohibition against testing the LORD (v.16), commands active obedience as the path to inheritance (vv.17–19), and closes with a model catechetical exchange in which salvation history becomes the answer to a child's question (vv.20–25).

**Translator patterns noted:**
- EMET is highly literal, preserving Hebrew word order and particles ("Slaves we were," "And righteousness it shall be for us"), using Hebrew place names (*Mitsrayim*, *Yisra'el*), and transliterating technical terms (*totafot*, *mezuzot*). Textual notes are rich and precise.
- LOGOS is formally equivalent with fluid English syntax, using English name forms (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Egypt), preserving the Deuteronomic legal triad ("statutes and judgments"), and offering careful theological annotation.
- PNEUMA is dynamic and smooth, favoring modern idiom ("with all your being," "Recite them"), grouping verses into continuous prose blocks, and making the single most consequential interpretive choice of the chapter: rendering *echad* as "alone" rather than "one" at v.4.

**Key rulings:**
- V.4 (*echad*): "one" not "alone." The LXX (*heis*), the Masoretic tradition, and the Synoptic citations of the Shema (Mark 12:29) all read "one." PNEUMA's "alone" is a defensible rendering but imports an exclusivity nuance that goes beyond the Hebrew — and departs from every major ancient witness. SOPHIA rules "one."
- V.5 (*nafshekha*): "soul" not "being." Consistency with the established Shema-vocabulary in Deuteronomy (cf. DEU 004 v.29 ruling).
- V.5 (*me'odekha*): "strength" — "might" (EMET/LOGOS) and "strength" (PNEUMA) are both adequate. SOPHIA adopts "strength" for slightly more natural rhythm in English.
- V.7 (*ve-shinnantam*): "teach them diligently." EMET's "repeat them sharply" is linguistically precise but awkward; LOGOS's "teach them diligently" and PNEUMA's "recite them" both smooth away the underlying metaphor of incision. SOPHIA adopts "teach them diligently" (LOGOS) as the best balance.
- V.8 (*totafot*): "frontlets [totafot]" — EMET's transliteration with gloss is preserved, following project convention for technical terms.
- V.12 ("house of slaves/slavery"): EMET: "house of slaves." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "house of slavery." The Hebrew *beit avadim* — "house of slaves." SOPHIA: "house of slaves" (EMET) — the concrete noun is preferable to the abstract.
- V.15 (*El qanna*): "a jealous God" — consistent with DEU 004 v.24 ruling.
- V.16 (testing formula): LOGOS "put the LORD your God to the test" over EMET's "test" — fuller, clearer.
- V.20 (*machar*): "in time to come" (LOGOS) over EMET's "tomorrow" — the idiom is well-established.
- V.22 (*ra'im*): "calamitous" (LOGOS) over EMET's "evil" — the signs are described from the Egyptian perspective; "calamitous" is more precise in this direction.
- V.25 (*tsedaqah*): "righteousness" — all three translators agree on this rendering; SOPHIA notes the important LXX divergence (*eleemosyne*) without adopting it.

The LXX (Codex Vaticanus, p. 148) is followed on the Shema structure. The LXX renders *totafot* as *asaleuton* ("immovable") — a remarkable interpretive reading. SOPHIA follows the MT with "frontlets [totafot]."

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** "Now this is the commandment — the statutes and the ordinances — that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, so that you may do them in the land to which you are crossing over to possess it,

**2** so that you may fear the LORD your God — you and your son and your son's son — by keeping all his statutes and his commandments that I am commanding you, all the days of your life; and so that your days may be long.

**3** Hear therefore, O Israel, and take care to do them, so that it may go well with you and that you may multiply greatly — as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has spoken to you — in a land flowing with milk and honey.

**4** Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.

**5** And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.

**6** And these words that I am commanding you today shall be on your heart.

**7** And you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way and when you lie down and when you rise up.

**8** And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets [totafot] between your eyes.

**9** And you shall write them on the doorposts [mezuzot] of your house and on your gates.

**10** And it shall be when the LORD your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers — to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob — to give you: great and good cities that you did not build,

**11** and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns hewn out that you did not hew, vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant — and you eat and are satisfied —

**12** then take care lest you forget the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slaves.

**13** The LORD your God you shall fear, and him you shall serve, and by his name you shall swear.

**14** You shall not go after other gods, from the gods of the peoples who are around you —

**15** for the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God — lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.

**16** You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.

**17** You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies and his statutes that he has commanded you.

**18** And you shall do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, so that it may go well with you and that you may go in and possess the good land that the LORD swore to your fathers —

**19** to thrust out all your enemies before you, as the LORD has spoken.

**20** When your son asks you in time to come, saying: "What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the ordinances that the LORD our God commanded you?" —

**21** you shall say to your son: "Slaves we were to Pharaoh in Egypt, and the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand.

**22** And the LORD gave great and calamitous signs and wonders against Egypt, against Pharaoh and against all his household, before our eyes.

**23** And he brought us out from there in order to bring us in, to give to us the land that he swore to our fathers.

**24** And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our lasting good, to keep us alive, as at this day.

**25** And it will be righteousness for us when we take care to do all this commandment before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us."

---

## Verse-by-Verse Ruling Notes

**V.1 — "ordinances" vs. "judgments":** EMET/PNEUMA: "ordinances." LOGOS: "judgments." Per established convention (*mishpatim* = "ordinances" in Deuteronomic legal context), SOPHIA: "ordinances."

**V.2 — structure:** EMET structures this as a purpose clause parallel to v.1; LOGOS and PNEUMA fold the generational language more smoothly. SOPHIA follows LOGOS's clean structure while retaining the Deuteronomic legal vocabulary.

**V.3 — "Hear therefore" vs. "And you shall hear":** EMET: "And you shall hear, O Yisra'el." LOGOS: "Hear therefore, O Israel." PNEUMA: "Hear, O Israel." The Hebrew *ve-shama'ta* is a waw-consecutive perfect — "and you shall hear" — functioning as a consequence or exhortation. SOPHIA: "Hear therefore" (LOGOS) — the "therefore" connects this verse's exhortation to the purpose clauses of vv.1–2 and anticipates the Shema of v.4.

**V.4 — echad ("one" vs. "alone"):** The single most consequential ruling in this chapter. EMET/LOGOS: "the LORD is one." PNEUMA: "The LORD alone." The Hebrew *echad* is the cardinal number "one." The LXX (Vaticanus p. 148): *Κύριος εἷς ἐστιν* — "the LORD is one" — using *heis* (one), not *monos* (alone). The Synoptic citations (Mark 12:29 following the LXX) read "one." The meaning "alone" would require *levado* or a different construction. SOPHIA: "the LORD is one" — the plain sense, the ancient witness, and the established liturgical rendering.

**V.5 — nafshekha ("soul" vs. "being"):** EMET/LOGOS: "with all your soul." PNEUMA: "with all your being." Consistent with DEU 004 ruling: *nefesh* in Shema-language = "soul." SOPHIA: "with all your soul."

**V.5 — me'odekha ("might" vs. "strength"):** EMET/LOGOS: "might." PNEUMA: "strength." Both are accurate renderings of this unusual substantive use of *me'od*. SOPHIA: "strength" — the slightly more natural English in this list.

**V.7 — shinnantam ("teach diligently" vs. "repeat sharply" vs. "recite"):** EMET: "repeat them sharply." LOGOS: "teach them diligently." PNEUMA: "Recite them." The Pi'el of *shanan* means to sharpen/incise — the image is of deep, repeated instruction. SOPHIA: "teach them diligently" (LOGOS) — captures the intensity without the awkwardness of "sharply" or the reduced force of "recite."

**V.8 — totafot:** All three preserve "frontlets." EMET adds the transliteration *totafot*; LOGOS does not. SOPHIA: "frontlets [totafot]" — per project convention of preserving Hebrew technical terms with bracketed gloss for hapax legomena.

**V.9 — mezuzot:** EMET preserves transliteration "doorposts [mezuzot]"; LOGOS: "doorposts"; PNEUMA: "doorposts." SOPHIA: "doorposts [mezuzot]" — the term is significant enough to warrant the gloss, as it became the name of a later practice.

**V.10 — verse structure (gift-list):** EMET maintains a long subordinate clause; LOGOS/PNEUMA work similarly. SOPHIA adopts LOGOS's clean structure with the apodosis ("great and good cities...") in apposition.

**V.12 — "house of slaves" vs. "house of slavery":** EMET: "house of slaves." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "house of slavery." Hebrew *beit avadim* = "house of slaves" (the concrete noun *avadim*). SOPHIA: "house of slaves" (EMET) — the concrete image of enslaved persons is preferable to the abstract.

**V.13 — word order:** EMET preserves the Hebrew inverted word order: "The LORD your God you shall fear, and him you shall serve." LOGOS/PNEUMA normalize. SOPHIA: retains the inverted order for the rhetorical emphasis — the fronted object ("The LORD your God") is the point.

**V.15 — El qanna:** EMET: "a jealous God [El qanna]." LOGOS: "a jealous God." PNEUMA: "a jealous God." All agree. SOPHIA: "a jealous God" — consistent with DEU 004 ruling.

**V.16 — "put to the test" vs. "test":** EMET: "You shall not test the LORD your God." LOGOS: "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test." PNEUMA: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test." SOPHIA: LOGOS's fuller formulation ("put...to the test") — the fuller phrase reflects the Hebrew verb *nasah* and avoids the archaic feel of "test the LORD."

**V.18 — "in the sight of" vs. "in the eyes of":** EMET: "in the eyes of the LORD." LOGOS: "in the sight of the LORD." PNEUMA: "in the LORD's sight." The Hebrew *be-einei YHWH* = "in the eyes of the LORD." SOPHIA: "in the sight of the LORD" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) — "the eyes of the LORD" (EMET) is literal; "in the sight of" is the established English idiom for this phrase in Deuteronomy.

**V.20 — "judgments/ordinances":** EMET: "ordinances." LOGOS: "judgments." PNEUMA: "ordinances." SOPHIA: "ordinances" — consistent with the ruling at v.1.

**V.20 — "in time to come" vs. "tomorrow":** EMET: "tomorrow." LOGOS: "in time to come." PNEUMA: "In the future." Hebrew *machar* can mean "tomorrow" literally or idiomatically "in time to come / in the future." In this catechetical context the idiomatic sense is clear. SOPHIA: "in time to come" (LOGOS) — the established rendering for this Passover-haggadah formula.

**V.21 — "strong hand" vs. "mighty hand":** EMET: "strong hand." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "mighty hand." Hebrew *yad chazaqah* — *chazaq* = strong/firm. Per project convention established at DEU 004 v.34: "strong hand" (EMET) for consistency with *chazaq*.

**V.22 — "signs and wonders" order and adjective:** EMET: "signs and wonders — great and evil." LOGOS: "signs and wonders, great and calamitous." PNEUMA: "great and devastating signs and wonders." Hebrew *otot u-mofetim gedolim ve-ra'im* — "signs and wonders, great and evil." The word *ra'im* (evil/terrible) modifies the signs from Egypt's perspective. SOPHIA: "great and calamitous signs and wonders" (LOGOS) — "calamitous" captures the destructive quality without importing a moral judgment that "evil" could ambiguously suggest.

**V.23 — "us he brought out" vs. "he brought us out":** EMET preserves the emphatic Hebrew word order: "And us he brought out from there." LOGOS/PNEUMA normalize. SOPHIA follows EMET's emphasis — the pronoun "us" (otanu) is fronted in Hebrew for rhetorical contrast with the fathers of v.23b.

**V.24 — "for our lasting good" vs. "for our good all the days":** EMET: "for our good all the days." LOGOS: "for our lasting good." PNEUMA: "for our own good always." Hebrew *le-tovah lanu kol ha-yamim* = "for good to us all the days." SOPHIA: "for our lasting good" (LOGOS) — a natural English compression that preserves the permanence of *kol ha-yamim*.

**V.25 — tsedaqah ("righteousness"):** All three translators agree: "righteousness." SOPHIA: "righteousness" — following MT (*tsedaqah*) rather than LXX (*eleemosyne* = almsgiving/mercy). The LXX divergence is noted in the textual record.

---

## Textual Notes for the Consensus Record

**V.4 — The Shema in ancient textual tradition:** The LXX Vaticanus (p. 148) renders: *Ἄκουε Ἰσραήλ· Κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν Κύριος εἷς ἐστιν* — "Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The addition of *ἐστιν* (is) as copula clarifies the predicative structure but is not in the MT. The NT (Mark 12:29) quotes this LXX form. The MT has no copula, leaving the syntax elegantly open. SOPHIA's rendering "the LORD our God, the LORD is one" supplies the implied copula while preserving both nominal clauses.

**V.5 — LXX expansion:** The LXX at v.5 reads *ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου* ("with all your mind") between the heart and soul clauses — an expansion not in the MT. The NT Synoptic citations (Matt 22:37; Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27) incorporate this expanded reading. SOPHIA follows the MT triad (heart, soul, strength).

**V.7 — Daily-life merism:** The four temporal markers — sitting, walking, lying down, rising up — constitute a merism covering all of daily existence. This is the ancient world's equivalent of "24/7." The command is total: Torah-speech is to permeate every waking and resting moment.

**V.8–9 — Tefillin and mezuzah:** These verses became the textual foundation for two major Jewish practices: binding phylacteries (*tefillin*) to hand and forehead (v.8) and affixing mezuzah scrolls to doorposts (v.9). The LXX renders *totafot* as *ἀσάλευτον* (immovable/unshakeable) — an interpretive reading that loses the physical object. SOPHIA follows the MT with "frontlets [totafot]."

**V.10–12 — The danger of gift:** This passage is one of Deuteronomy's most incisive theological warnings: prosperity is more spiritually dangerous than hardship. Israel did not build these cities, fill these houses, or hew these cisterns — and it is precisely when people receive what they did not earn that forgetting occurs. The parenetic structure (gift → warning → exhortation) is characteristic of the Deuteronomic homilist.

**V.13 — Positive oath obligation:** "By his name you shall swear" is a positive command — lawful oaths are made in the LORD's name, not by other gods. This stands in deliberate tension with later traditions discouraging oaths (Matt 5:34), but within Deuteronomy it asserts the LORD's exclusive claim over all sacred speech-acts.

**V.16 — Massah:** The reference to Massah (Exod 17:7, from *nasah* = to test) anchors the prohibition historically. Israel tested the LORD by demanding water; the remembered failure becomes the paradigm case of what must not be repeated. This verse is cited by Jesus in the wilderness temptation (Matt 4:7 / Luke 4:12).

**V.20–25 — The catechetical frame:** The question-and-answer structure here — a son's question evoking a father's recitation of salvation history — is the structural prototype of the Passover haggadah. The answer in vv.21–25 moves from bondage (v.21) to mighty act (v.22) to gift of land (v.23) to command (v.24) to righteousness (v.25): the full arc of covenantal theology in five verses.

**V.25 — tsedaqah vs. eleemosyne:** The MT *tsedaqah* (righteousness, covenant-conforming rightness) is rendered by the LXX as *ἐλεημοσύνη* (almsgiving/mercy) — a striking interpretive shift that influenced the Greek-speaking Jewish and early Christian understanding of "righteousness as charity." SOPHIA follows the MT; the LXX variant is preserved in the record as a significant textual datum.
